title_en.v1.title: Oil Pulling in 10–20 Minutes: Coconut or Sesame Oil for Oral Care and Claimed Detox Benefits
title_en.v1.reason: The transcript clearly identifies oil pulling, the oils used, duration and the video's claimed benefits.

detailed_summary.v3.overview: The video presents oil pulling as a daily morning practice: place about one tablespoon of coconut, sesame or another cold-pressed oil in the mouth on an empty stomach, swish it for 10–20 minutes, then spit it out and brush normally. The creator describes oil pulling as a traditional Indian natural-healing technique and explains it using the idea that oral microorganisms have lipid membranes that can associate with oil. The video then goes far beyond oral hygiene, claiming that oil pulling removes toxins from the entire body and can help conditions ranging from acne and constipation to arthritis, asthma, insomnia, hypertension, migraines, gray hair and fat loss. Those systemic and curative claims are not demonstrated by the package and should be treated as source claims. Practical precautions stated in the video are not to swallow the used oil and not to spit it into a sink because it may clog pipes. The most defensible practical takeaway is the clearly described oil-pulling routine, while the broad detox and disease claims require substantial caution.

title_en.v1.title: One-Day Fasting as a Body Reset: Benefits, Ekadashi Timing, Hydration and Breaking the Fast
title_en.v1.reason: The transcript centers on fasting, its claimed benefits, practical methods, Ekadashi timing and how to break a fast.

detailed_summary.v3.overview: The video argues that voluntary fasting differs from starvation and presents fasting as an old religious and health practice found across several traditions. It blends Ayurvedic concepts with references to modern fasting research and claims benefits including cellular cleanup, weight control, metabolic changes and improved cognition. The transcript discusses myths about fasting lowering metabolism or causing muscle loss, then moves to practical options ranging from lighter-food days to coconut-water or water fasting. It suggests choosing a level appropriate to the individual and mentions that longer or stricter fasts should be done with guidance. The speaker places special value on Ekadashi as a traditional fasting day and advises breaking a fast gently with lemon water, fruit and then normal food. Practical tips include drinking warm water when hungry and eating a lighter dinner beforehand. Because the transcript is partially corrupted and several scientific claims are simplified or exaggerated, the safest interpretation is as a traditional wellness perspective rather than definitive medical guidance.

title_en.v1.title: Liver Cleanse Claims: Sugarcane Juice, Bhringrajasava, Kutki and Supportive Foods
title_en.v1.reason: The transcript clearly identifies three main remedies plus supporting foods and lifestyle advice.

detailed_summary.v3.overview: The video explains the liver's detoxification role, lists signs the creator associates with poor liver function, reviews lifestyle factors said to burden the liver and recommends three Ayurvedic-style interventions. The first is fresh sugarcane juice for about 15 days, optionally with ginger and lemon, taken before breakfast or several hours after lunch. The second is Bhringrajasava, described as a classical formulation; the video recommends four teaspoons mixed with four teaspoons of water once daily after breakfast or lunch. The third is Kutki powder, suggested at half a teaspoon with half a teaspoon of honey about an hour before breakfast for 15 days. The video also promotes turmeric, fenugreek, ginger, jaggery, grapes, pears, lemon, coconut, amla, whole grains, leafy vegetables, nuts, seeds, beetroot and carrots, together with reducing alcohol, smoking, packaged foods and sleep deprivation. Importantly, several symptoms mentioned—yellow skin/eyes, dark urine, swelling, appetite loss and easy bruising—can be medically significant; the video should not be used to diagnose or treat liver disease without clinical evaluation.

title_en.v1.title: What Happens During a 36-Hour Fast: Glycogen, Ketosis, Autophagy, Risks and Refeeding
title_en.v1.reason: The transcript explicitly follows metabolic changes during a 36-hour fast and includes contraindications and refeeding advice.

detailed_summary.v3.overview: This animated educational video follows a fictional person considering a 36-hour fast and uses talking organs to explain the proposed metabolic sequence. Early in the fast, the body uses glucose and stored liver glycogen; the video states roughly 100 g of glycogen and suggests it can cover about 10–12 hours. As glycogen declines, insulin falls, glucagon rises and fat use increases. The animation then introduces ketosis and beta-hydroxybutyrate, followed later by autophagy as cellular recycling. It also claims improvements in blood pressure, inflammation, insulin sensitivity, cholesterol, neuroplasticity and oxidative stress, although the timing and magnitude of several claims are simplified. Importantly, the closing section gives clear safety warnings: extended fasting is not recommended without guidance for children, pregnant people, people with eating disorders, health conditions or medications. It also notes risks such as electrolyte imbalance, disturbed sleep and post-fast digestive problems, recommends hydration and advises breaking the fast gently with easy foods rather than a large meal.

title_en.v1.title: Ayurvedic 'Blood Purification' Claims: Neem Leaves, Manjisthadi Kwath and Lifestyle Changes
title_en.v1.reason: The transcript clearly centers on Ayurvedic blood-purification ideas and identifies neem leaves and Manjisthadi/Mahamanjisthadi preparations.

detailed_summary.v3.overview: The video uses the traditional Ayurvedic idea of rakt shodhana or blood purification to explain recurring skin and wellness problems. It argues that internal factors, diet, pollution, stress and lifestyle habits can burden systems involved in elimination and that reducing those burdens may help overall health. The transcript clearly identifies fresh neem leaves as one suggested short-term approach and also mentions Manjisthadi or Mahamanjisthadi Kwath, a classical Ayurvedic formulation containing herbs such as manjistha, neem and giloy. It also encourages simpler food, reduced heavily processed or spicy foods, attention to meal timing, fasting-like digestive rest and yoga or mental calm. Because the transcript is heavily corrupted, exact dosing for some preparations is not reliable enough to reproduce. More importantly, the framing that eczema, psoriasis or other conditions primarily reflect 'impure blood' is not medically precise and should not delay evidence-based diagnosis or treatment.
